Evaluation of watershed-level runoff against river gauge data

Miquel De Cáceres / María González

2026-11-20

Source: vignettes/evaluation/WatershedLevelEvaluation.Rmd
WatershedLevelEvaluation.Rmd

Introduction

Goal

The aim of this article is to provide an assessment of the predictive performance of spwb_land() and growth_land() for the prediction of watershed outflow. To this aim, we simulate hydrological processes in a set of benchmark watersheds and compare the model predictions of watershed outflow against measurements obtained using river gauges at watershed outlets. Simulations are performed after calibrating watershed-level hydrological parameters with a subset of observations. The vignette also includes estimates of computation time for each watershed under different models and control parameters.

Calibration and simulation

For each watershed, the following procedure has been conducted:

  1. Initial warm-up simulation with default parameters for a specified number of years, aimed to fill the aquifer and equilibrate soils.
  2. Calibration of watershed parameters for a specific period (warm-up + analysis) using a genetic algorithm and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) as optimization function. Calibration is conducted with the same function (either spwb_land() or growth_land() to be used in evaluation).
  3. Simulation with calibrated watershed parameters for the whole period, that includes both the calibration period and a later period used for independent evaluation.

Both in the calibration procedure and the final simulations with calibrated parameters, the vegetation input has been aggregated into size classes, for computational simplicity.

Evaluation

For each watershed, simulation results are compared to observed watershed outflow, differentiating between the period used for calibration and a posterior period used for independent evaluation.

Time series

A comparison of observed vs. simulated (with spwb_land() or growth_land()) time series is shown, at the daily and monthly scales.

Goodness-of-fit statistics

The following goodness of fit statistics are calculated using package hydroGOF:

  • Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE): This coefficient is sensitive to extreme values and might yield sub-optimal results when the dataset contains large outliers.
  • Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE): Provides a decomposition of the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency, which facilitates the analysis of the importance of different components (bias, correlation and variability).
  • Index of agreement (d): Initially proposed by Willmott (1981) to overcome the drawbacks of the R2, such as the differences in observed and predicted means and variances (Legates and McCabe, 1999). d is also dimensionless and bounded between 0 and 1 and can be interpreted similarly to R2.
  • Volumetric efficiency index (VE): Originally proposed by Criss and Winston (2008) to circumvent some of the NSE flaws. VE values are also bounded [0, 1] and represent the fraction of water delivered at the proper time.
  • Root mean squared error (RMSE): The usual estimation of average model error (i.e. the square root of mean squared errors).

Hydrological analysis

The density distribution and percentiles of daily discharge are compared between observations and predictions, for both the calibration and evaluation periods.

Computation times

For each watershed, we provide a table of computation times in seconds corresponding to 30-day simulations of watershed processes, with either spwb_land() or growth_land(). Different combinations of control parameters are tested for transpirationMode (either Granier or Sureau), rhizosphereOverlap (either total or partial) or soilDomains (either single or dual). Different degrees of vegetation detail are also tested: (a) tree-level original inventory records; (b) aggregation of trees and shrubs into size classes; (c) simplification to the dominant tree/shrub species.
